source_text: TMP-9021 Action Item Recommendation to approve an interlocal agreement between Reno-Sparks Indian Colony ("RSIC" or "Tribe") and Washoe County, by and through Washoe County Regional Animal Services ("WCRAS"), with a term of three years ; and authorize the Chair of the Board of County Commissioners to execute the agreement. Under this agreement, WCRAS will provide certain animal control and sheltering services for the benefit of the Tribe, including impoundment and care of stray/lost dogs and cats found on Reservation property; disposition of unclaimed dogs and cats; quarantine of dogs and cats that have bitten a person; safehold of dogs and cats in the event of an owner's death; limited field services; and yearly outreach (vaccination) services, with costs to be borne by Tribe as specified in Exhibit A. It is further recommended to authorize the Director of WCRAS to approve and execute annual addendums with amendments to Exhibit A (Costs & Fees) and Article 11 (Notices) as necessary. source_text: TMP-9246 Action Item Declaration of canvass of local results of General Election 2024 and direction to the Registrar of Voters to certify the abstract of the results and transmit a copy of the certified abstract to the Secretary of State. Canvassing is the process by which local election results are declared, examined and certified. The canvass is a culmination of all the data generated during an election cycle. The canvass process aggregates and confirms every valid ballot cast and counted, including mail, uniformed and overseas citizen, electronically transmitted ballots, early voting, and Election Day ballots. NRS 293.387 requires the Board of County Commissioners to separately note any clerical errors discovered and take account of those errors, so the result declared represents the true vote cast. Pursuant to NRS 293.387, the Board of County Commissioners is required to canvass the vote and direct an abstract of votes to be sent to the Secretary of State no later than 10 days following the election, which was held on November 5, 2024. source_snippet: TMP-9630 Action Item Request by the Washoe County Manager, through the Washoe County Clerk, and pursuant to Washoe County Code (“WCC”) 2.030, to initiate amendments to WCC Chapter 5 (Administration and Personnel) to update provisions relating to citizen advisory boards (CABs). The amendments may include, but are not limited to: renaming the boards; clarifying that the purpose of the boards is to provide feedback on community-wide issues within Washoe County’s governmental jurisdiction as part of the commissioner support program; requiring the geographical boundaries of the boards to fall within a single commissioner district; updating provisions for appointment of members; removing the prohibition on CAB members from concurrently serving on the County’s planning commission or board of adjustment; amending various provisions to comply with current open meeting law requirements; and upd...
source_text: TMP-9630 Action Item Request by the Washoe County Manager, through the Washoe County Clerk, and pursuant to Washoe County Code (“WCC”) 2.030, to initiate amendments to WCC Chapter 5 (Administration and Personnel) to update provisions relating to citizen advisory boards (CABs). The amendments may include, but are not limited to: renaming the boards; clarifying that the purpose of the boards is to provide feedback on community-wide issues within Washoe County’s governmental jurisdiction as part of the commissioner support program; requiring the geographical boundaries of the boards to fall within a single commissioner district; updating provisions for appointment of members; removing the prohibition on CAB members from concurrently serving on the County’s planning commission or board of adjustment; amending various provisions to comply with current open meeting law requirements; and updating provisions related to bylaws; and direct the County Clerk to submit the request to the District Attorney’s Office for preparation of a proposed ordinance in accordance with WCC 2.040. source_text: TMP-10190 Public Hearing Public Hearing: For possible action to conduct a Public Hearing under the Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act ("TEFRA") and adopt a resolution approving the issuance by the National Finance Authority (New Hampshire) of not to exceed $33,000,000 of Lease Revenue Bonds on behalf of NCCS-UNR Fieldhouse Properties LLC (the "Borrower") for purposes of, and as required by, Internal Revenue Code of 1986 Section 147(f), as amended. The bonds or a portion thereof will be "private activity bonds" and "qualified 501(c)(3) bonds" for purposes of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. The revenue from the bond issuance will be used (a) finance the cost of the design, development, construction and equipping of (i) an approximately 73,700 square foot indoor all sport fieldhouse and related amenities, (ii) an approximately 85,796 square foot outdoor turf football practice field, and (iii) an approximately 106,078 square foot turf intermural field to be located on the campus of the University of Nevada, Reno (collectively, including related site development, utility, equipment and other improvements Not available Not available

source_text: TMP-10280 Resolution Recommendation to accept a 2026 Nevada State Emergency Response Commission (SERC), United We Stand (UWS) grant for [$32,000.00 no County match required]. The UWS grant is intended to improve state and local government planning, training, and response capabilities to react to Acts of Terrorism. If approved, authorize the Local Emergency Planning Committee (LEPC) Chair to execute grant documents and authorize the County Manager or their designee, to sign the Washoe County Sub-Grant Agreements between Washoe County and REMSA Health, per NRS 244.1505 in the amount of [$5,128.00] for one (1) Tactical Rope Access and Rescue Equipment; the Reno Police Department, per NRS 244.1505 in the amount of [$9,318.00] for twelve (12) Avon Protection Voice Unit Gen with Microphone; and Sparks Police Department, per NRS 244.1505, in the amount of [$10,000.00] for four (4) PepperBall Launchers; approve Resolution necessary for same; and direct Finance to make the necessary budget amendments. Project Manager Kevin Selstrum detailed plans to improve the TRI Sheriff’s Office Substation. source_text: 4. Recommended Conditions of Approval A. Special Use Permit. This approval is for Special Use Permit 2026-018 to construct a natural gas fueled electrical generating facility. The electricity generated will be used on adjacent properties owned and/or controlled by the applicant. The project includes onsite storage of compressed natural gas (CNG). The property is located within the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center at 2300 Peru Drive, McCarran, Storey County, NV, Assessor’s Parcel Number 005-012-73. B. Requirements. source_snippet: 2. Representatives of the Union and its affiliates will be permitted to transact Union business on County property, provided that this does not disrupt normal work functions. In accordance with NRS 288, the Employer may require Union business to be conducted during non-work time, such as before work and after work, during breaks, and/or lunchtime. Union business may only be conducted in common areas and/or designated Employee break areas. The designated representative of the Union shall be allowed to receive telephone calls or other communique concerning Union business at any time during working hours. The Union shall have the right to use the interoffice mail for Union business. County email may be used internally to conduct Union business but shall be limited to all parties to this Agreement and subject to established County policies.
source_text: 2. Representatives of the Union and its affiliates will be permitted to transact Union business on County property, provided that this does not disrupt normal work functions. In accordance with NRS 288, the Employer may require Union business to be conducted during non-work time, such as before work and after work, during breaks, and/or lunchtime. Union business may only be conducted in common areas and/or designated Employee break areas. The designated representative of the Union shall be allowed to receive telephone calls or other communique concerning Union business at any time during working hours. The Union shall have the right to use the interoffice mail for Union business. The agreed upon contract covers many benefits which will support the current members along with providing for an attractive package for future recruitment of new members to the Fire District. source_text: • Recommended motion: I, Commissioner (name), move to approve the Interlocal contract and referenced FY 2027 and FY 2028 budgets, as presented. • Prepared by: Maxine Cortes Department: Clerk & Treasurer Contact Number: (775) 283-7249 • Staff Summary: Since 2007, the First Judicial District Court has requested reimbursement from the State of Nevada acting by and through its Department of Health and Human Services to allow Carson City's General Fund to be reimbursed for child support enforcement services conducted in Carson City in lieu of requiring Carson City and Storey County residents to seek enforcement of child support matters in Reno, Nevada. The First Judicial District Court appoints a Child Support Magistrate to preside over the hearings. The Court's Marshals Division provides courtroom security and public screening, and court employees process child support documents. The hearings are conducted at the Murphy-Bernardini Regional Juvenile Justice Center. Every four years, a new Interlocal contract must be agreed upon to continue services and to allow Carson City to receive reimbursement. source_text: 13.118.010 Definitions. As used in this chapter, unless the context otherwise requires: "County resident" refers to any individual whose primary and legal place of residence is located within the geographical boundaries of Storey County. Residency may be demonstrated through documentation such as a valid driver’s license or state ID with a Storey County address, a current utility bill, lease or mortgage agreement, voter registration, or other official documents showing name and address within the Storey County. “Immediate Family” means the Storey County Resident’s spouse or domestic partner, parents, children (including stepchildren and legally adopted children), siblings, grandparents, and grandchildren, whether related by blood, marriage, or legal adoption. "Park" means any area designed by the county commissioners as a public park, playground or recreational facility pursuant to Section 13.118.050 of this chapter. source_text: 13.118.040 Compliance required. A. No person shall enter, be or remain in any park or swimming pool of the county as designated by the county commissioners by resolution pursuant to this chapter unless he/she complies they comply with this chapter and the regulations promulgated by this chapter and any resolution adopted pursuant thereto. B. The Storey County sheriff is authorized to eject and expel from a park and the swimming pool any person who violates the provisions of this chapter or any other law, ordinance, or park resolution that may be in effect at the time of such violation. C. Ejected or Expelled Persons. No person who has been ejected or expelled under the provisions of this section shall refuse to leave any park or swimming pool as ordered nor shall the person return to the park or swimming pool within twenty-four hours of such ejection or expulsion without the permission of the Storey County sheriff. D. Violation: Penalty. Any person who violates the provisions contained in this chapter or any park resolution adopted pursuant thereto is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars, imprisonment not to exceed six months, or both....

source_snippet: 4. Staff summary: This resolution is in recognition of the lifesaving efforts made by Storey County Fire District Firefighter Jesse Richardson. On July 26th Jesse responded along with his partner Charlie Bowman to a fire on Lousetown Road with a report of a victim trapped. While Charlie attempted access to the interior of the structure, Jesse carried a 24’ ladder around to the C side of the structure locating the victim on the balcony. He placed the ladder and even utilized a rock to stabilize it due to the angle. He then ascended the ladder and assisted the resident over the railing and down to safety. Without his efforts, the outcome could have been fatal.
source_text: 4. Staff summary: This resolution is in recognition of the lifesaving efforts made by Storey County Fire District Firefighter Jesse Richardson. On July 26th Jesse responded along with his partner Charlie Bowman to a fire on Lousetown Road with a report of a victim trapped. While Charlie attempted access to the interior of the structure, Jesse carried a 24’ ladder around to the C side of the structure locating the victim on the balcony. He placed the ladder and even utilized a rock to stabilize it due to the angle. He then ascended the ladder and assisted the resident over the railing and down to safety. Without his efforts, the outcome could have been fatal.

source_text: III. Conclusion For these reasons, Sunny Hills respectfully requests that the County decline to process or consider the SUP Application unless and until NV Energy demonstrates that it has obtained the requisite property owner authorizations for all affected properties. At a minimum, the County should continue consideration of the SUP Application until NV Energy identifies with specificity the parcels through which the Mira Loma Corridor is proposed to pass and the corresponding property interests necessary for the Project. Although the Commission should decline to consider the application, if it is nonetheless inclined to approve the application, the condition should go further. Not only should the SUP be conditioned on no construction proceeding without an easement or authorization, but the SUP should be revokable if NV Energy does not obtain the necessary property interests. The property owners should have the right to contest the SUP and petition it be revoked to remove the encumbrance on their properties. Sunny Hills further requests that this correspondence and the objections set forth herein be incorporated into the administrative record and considered by the Planning Comm...

It is in Chapter 5, which doesn’t really have anything to do with Planning, but the code talks a little bit about land uses. Main St. The Preliminary Plat for Great Basin Estates was also approved, and the Final Plat for that subdivision will go on the June 14, 2016 Meeting. source_text: recommendation to the Redevelopment Agency to establish a storefront improvement reimbursement program. As you know we did have that storefront program, it was a grant program that was federally funded. It was de-obligated from the funds by City Council. They have reached out to the Redevelopment Agency of Nevada and have meeting with them quarterly. There are several communities in the state that have done these storefront improvement reimbursement programs. They are going to reach out to them and get as much information from them as possible and learn from their trial and errors. The Redevelopment Advisory Council recommended to the Redevelopment Agency a program of $50,000 a year maximum expenditure up to five years, reevaluate the program at the five years. They also recommended a maximum of $10,000 reimbursement per property owner. That will go to the RDA at 2:30 pm on August 9, 2016. If that parcel wanted to have a zone change it wouldn’t be possible for that particular parcel, because of the area requirement. Step Three: If the grievance is not resolved at Step Two of the procedure, and the grievant desires to submit the dispute to the Yerington City Council for final resolution, the time for his/her appeal shall begin with the receipt of the response of the Yerington City Manager. Within thirty (30) calendar days of receipt of the written answer by the Yerington City Manager, the aggrieved party may appeal the decision to the Yerington City Council filing with the Yerington City Clerk a written statement of his/her intention to appeal, including sufficient details of circumstances surrounding the grievance. Grievance appeals shall be heard by the Yerington City Council and their finding shall be final and conclusive. Following notice of appeal, the Yerington City Clerk shall immediately notify the Mayor of the City of Yerington. If the date of the next regularly scheduled meeting of the Council is more than fifteen (15) calendar days from the date of the appeal is filed, the appeal shall be heard at the earliest possible date established by the Council.

source_text: 15. For Discussion Only: Discussion of Resolution 2026-07, a Resolution amending the City of Yerington Fee Schedule Water Standpipe Rates. This item was first publicly discussed by Yerington City Council at the March 23, 2026 regular meeting. Interim City Manager Bryant discusses the recently approved meter system. We hope to see this implemented soon to help streamline our services. This item is to consider amending the fee schedule to reflect a $5.00 per thousand gallon model at the J-stand water distribution location. Currently, we charge $38.00 for the first fifteen thousand gallons and a commodity rate of just over $2 per thousand gallons thereafter. Bryant proposes removing this model and going to the flat $5.00 per thousand gallons. Mr. Bryant also suggests adding a $100 start-up fee for new accounts to account for the time and staff spent on creating new accounts. Additionally, reactivating a PIN or re-opening after an account lockout for things such as non-payment will now incur a $25.00 fee. -- 25 of 61 -- There was no further discussion on this item.

source_text: 12. For Discussion Only: Discussion and Possible Action to adopt Resolution 2026-07, a Resolution amending the City of Yerington Fee Schedule Water Standpipe Rates. This item was first publicly discussed by Yerington City Council at the March 23, 2026 regular meeting and was previously heard by City Council on May 11, 2026. Interim City Manager states this is the third time this proposal has been presented to the council. Proposing changing the rates for J-Stand which include implementing a $100.00 startup fee and a $25.00 fee for a new pin entry or repining. New water fee will be $5.00 per thousand gallons, beginning with the first thousand gallons. This displaced the current structure of $38.00 for the first 15,000 gallons. Councilman Beaton made a motion to approve item number 12 as presented seconded by Councilman Lopez. Mayor Garry called for public comment, none was given, and the motion was approved unanimously

source_text: 7. For Presentation Only: Recognition of the Yerington Animal Shelter, on behalf of Best Friends Animal Society. Presented by Public Works Director Paul Shapiro. Public Works Director Paul Shapiro presented this item, stating it is the second consecutive year that the Yerington Animal Shelter was presented with this award by Best Friends Animal Society. It recognizes our shelter for achieving a 90% or better save rate with animals. While our shelter is not truly a “no-kill” shelter by ordinance, our staff and volunteers work diligently to find successful outcomes for all animals in our care. While not all can be saved, often due to health-related issues, our staff and volunteers work extremely hard to save them. This reflects the hard work of our staff, especially Ron Durst, who also works hard to resolve the prominent stray cat issue in our community. Mr. Durst spends many hours of his own time rescuing, transporting and releasing feral cats after they have been treated, spayed and neutered to help naturally and humanely reduce the population.

source_text: 8. For Possible Action: Discussion and Possible Action to Adopt Resolution 2026-11 authorizing the transfer of $6,427.00 for FY2026-2027 from Management/City Hall to Animal Control, within the General Fund, as authorized by NRS 354.598005. -- 27 of 99 -- Manager Bryant presented this item, stating that every weekend Public Works staff is paid overtime to manage the operations at the animal shelter. Additionally, there were budgeted funds for a part time employee at City Hall, that are no longer intended to be utilized. This transfer, if approved, would shift those part time employee funds to the animal shelter to allow the hire of a part time employee to manage the day to day cleaning, reducing the overtime expense incurred and free up Public Works staff to address other matters. Councilman Martin made a motion to approve as presented, second by Councilman Lopez. Mayor Garry requested public comment at this time, none was given. Item passed unanimously.

source_text: The 2025–2030 Comprehensive Economic Development Strategy charts a path that is both realistic about challenges and ambitious about opportunities. The Pumpkin Hollow mine restart, led by Kinterra Capital/Southwest Critical Materials, represents the most significant near-term economic catalyst—with the potential to add hundreds of high-wage jobs, stimulate a local supply chain, and generate tax revenues supporting community infrastructure. Alongside this, the diversification of agriculture, expansion of tourism along the Walker River, investment in downtown revitalization, and targeted workforce development programs will collectively strengthen the economic foundation. Success will require sustained collaboration among the City of Yerington, Lyon County, the Western Nevada Development District, the Yerington Paiute Tribe, major employers, educational institutions, and state and federal partners. (For Possible Action) CIO Misty Rowley explained that during the implementation of Ironclad they discovered they needed more power user licenses to cover multiple people in the offices. They started with 20 users, and the increase will bring them to 32. CIO Rowley also requested the Board approve her to add or remove licenses as necessary. Commissioner Plaskett motioned to approve the addition of 12 Ironclad Power User licenses at a rate of $600 per user per year to the existing three-year term (January 20, 2026 through September 1, 2028). source_text: meeting. (For Possible Action) CIO Misty Rowley explained that during the implementation of Ironclad they discovered they needed more power user licenses to cover multiple people in the offices. They started with 20 users, and the increase will bring them to 32. CIO Rowley also requested the Board approve her to add or remove licenses as necessary. Commissioner Plaskett motioned to approve the addition of 12 Ironclad Power User licenses at a rate of $600 per user per year to the existing three-year term (January 20, 2026 through September 1, 2028). Also to authorize CIO Rowley to add or remove licenses as necessary and to execute the Order Form outside of the meeting. Commissioner Schoenwald seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0. COUNTY FACILITIES – Brenna Rogne, Facilities/Events Manager

source_text: 3. Review, discuss and provide direction to the Comptroller related to proposed cost of living adjustments for Non-PERS and PERS employees, effective July 5, 2026. Note: Union contracts have not been approved for next year so COLA increase is unknown at this time. Elected Officials are limited to a 2% increase, County Commissioners are limited to a 3% increase. (For Possible The County Elected Officials are limited to a 2% cost of living adjustment (COLA) increase and the County Commissioners are limited to a 3% increase. The Board discussed a 3% increase for hourly employees, a $0.25 increase for casuals and chose to not take an increase for the Commissioners. Commissioner Schoenwald motioned to approve a 0% cost of living adjustment (COLA) increase for the Commissioners, 2% COLA for elected officials, 3% COLA for hourly employees and $0.25 increase for casual positions. Commissioner Plaskett seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0.

(For Possible Action) The Sheriff’s office was using Trans Union Risk and Alternative for background checks and investigations; Trans Union was more eastern based and cost $1,100 monthly. Thompson Reuters is western based and will cost $211 monthly. Commissioner Schoenwald motioned to approve entering into a 3-year contract with Thompson Reuters (Clear for LE, investigative resource) in the amount of $211.00 a month for the first year with a 5% increase in years 2 & 3 and authorize the Sheriff’s Department to sign contract outside of the meeting. source_text: Thompson Reuters will replace Trans Union Risk and Alternative. (For Possible Action) The Sheriff’s office was using Trans Union Risk and Alternative for background checks and investigations; Trans Union was more eastern based and cost $1,100 monthly. Thompson Reuters is western based and will cost $211 monthly. Commissioner Schoenwald motioned to approve entering into a 3-year contract with Thompson Reuters (Clear for LE, investigative resource) in the amount of $211.00 a month for the first year with a 5% increase in years 2 & 3 and authorize the Sheriff’s Department to sign contract outside of the meeting. Commissioner Plaskett seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0. ROAD DEPARTMENT – Scooter Mentaberry, Supervisor

(Discussion) EMS Director/Coordinator Nichole Cooley, EMT Griffan Bussian and EMT Brent Jones reported the total runs for January were 25 with Eureka having 15, Crescent Valley 10 and they brought in $8,028.94. For January the dentist had 36 patients, Genesis home health had 18, the Eureka clinic saw 338 patients with Pena seeing 139, Kleinman 136, Harper 4, Rocky 10 and MA 49. The Crescent Valley clinic saw 17 patients. EMT Bussian reported they are working with their Aspire students and went to the high school and held a Q&A with the sophomore class. EMT Bussian reported on the new procedures and medications that they are now able to provide. source_text: 1. Review, discuss and provide direction to the Comptroller related to proposed cost of living adjustments for Non-PERS and PERS employees, effective July 5, 2026. Note: Union contracts have not been approved for next year so COLA increase is unknown at this time. Elected Officials are limited to a 2% increase, County Commissioners are limited to a 3% increase. (For Possible Action) At the previous Commission meeting during the budget session the board chose to not approve a COLA increase for the County Commissioners, Comptroller Kim Todd informed the board that due to a new legislative bill they unfortunately can not approve some but not all. In order to follow new legislature the board either approves a COLA increase for all non-PERS and PERS employees, elected officials and County Commissioners or none at all. Commissioner Schoenwald motioned to approve a 2% COLA for elected officials, 3% for County Commissioners, 3% COLA for hourly employees and $0.25 increase for casual positions. Commissioner Plaskett seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0.

source_snippet: (For Possible Action) The proposed changes to the Eureka County Personnel Policy: Leave Plans, 6.1 Holidays are: Employees participating in the 4x10 pilot program shall follow the existing Holiday Leave policy applicable to 10-hour workdays, except as modify below. For Offices required by Nevada law to remain operational, including elected official offices: If a federally recognized holiday falls on a Friday or Saturday, the elected official or department head may coordinate with employees to schedule an alternate day off. Any such holiday leave must be taken within the same work week in which the holiday occurs, ensuring that operational coverage is maintained. Commissioner Plaskett motioned to approve the changes to Eureka County Personnel Policy: Leave Plans, 6.1 Holidays. Commissioner Schoenwald seconded the motion. The motion carried 3- IT – Misty Rowley, CIO

Any such holiday leave must be taken within the same work week in which the holiday occurs, ensuring that operational coverage is maintained. Commissioner Plaskett motioned to approve the changes to Eureka County Personnel Policy: Leave Plans, 6.1 Holidays. Commissioner Schoenwald seconded the motion. source_text: 1. Report on current and emerging natural resource issues affecting Eureka County. (Discussion) Natural Resources Manager Jake Tibbitts reported the Rodent Board met and approved the borough builder rental agreement; members of the Rodent District can now come and rent the borough builder. The Rodent Board also approved a few cost share reimbursements. Manager Tibbitts attended the BLM Greater Sage Grouse Plan Implementation meeting with cooperating agencies; they are committed to developing a Memorandum of Understandings with the State and NDOW to clarify some of the grey areas moving forward. Manager Tibbitts gave a presentation to the Diamond Valley Groundwater Management Plan on the results of the Mining and Land Resource -- 12 of 299 -- Page 9 of 11- April 21, 2026 Institute meeting. Manager Tibbitts attended a meeting with ORLA Mining about the South Railroad project, they discussed the concerns Pine Valley residents had on the water issues, he believes they will be removing their protests on the water applications. Manager Tibbitts reminded the board Firewise days will be May 1st in Eureka and May 2nd in Crescent Valley.

(For Possible Action) Senior Center Program Director Linda Gordon presented to the board sending a letter to Nevada Department of Transportation forgoing the FTA Section 5310, FEY25-26 Funding Application Operating Assistance 50/50 grant. For the County to get full use of the grant they would have to spend $6,000 a month on maintenance to the senior vans. source_text: Operating Assistance 50/50 grant. Commissioner Schoenwald motioned to approve Senior Center Program Director Linda Gordon sending a letter to Nevada Department of Transportation forgoing the FTA Section 5310, FEY25-26 Funding Application Operating Assistance 50/50 grant. Commissioner Plaskett seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0. THE EUREKA SENTINEL- Ben Rowley, Owner/ Publisher

source_snippet: meeting. (For Possible Action) CIO Misty Rowley explained that during the implementation of Ironclad they discovered they needed more power user licenses to cover multiple people in the offices. They started with 20 users, and the increase will bring them to 32. CIO Rowley also requested the Board approve her to add or remove licenses as necessary. Commissioner Plaskett motioned to approve the addition of 12 Ironclad Power User licenses at a rate of $600 per user per year to the existing three-year term (January 20, 2026 through September 1, 2028). Also to authorize CIO Rowley to add or remove licenses as necessary and to execute the Order Form outside of the meeting. Commissioner Schoenwald seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0. COUNTY FACILITIES – Brenna Rogne, Facilities/Events Manager
source_text: meeting. (For Possible Action) CIO Misty Rowley explained that during the implementation of Ironclad they discovered they needed more power user licenses to cover multiple people in the offices. They started with 20 users, and the increase will bring them to 32. CIO Rowley also requested the Board approve her to add or remove licenses as necessary. Commissioner Plaskett motioned to approve the addition of 12 Ironclad Power User licenses at a rate of $600 per user per year to the existing three-year term (January 20, 2026 through September 1, 2028). Also to authorize CIO Rowley to add or remove licenses as necessary and to execute the Order Form outside of the meeting. Commissioner Schoenwald seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0. COUNTY FACILITIES – Brenna Rogne, Facilities/Events Manager

Commissioner Plaskett seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0.

source_text: Thompson Reuters will replace Trans Union Risk and Alternative. (For Possible Action) The Sheriff’s office was using Trans Union Risk and Alternative for background checks and investigations; Trans Union was more eastern based and cost $1,100 monthly. Thompson Reuters is western based and will cost $211 monthly. Commissioner Schoenwald motioned to approve entering into a 3-year contract with Thompson Reuters (Clear for LE, investigative resource) in the amount of $211.00 a month for the first year with a 5% increase in years 2 & 3 and authorize the Sheriff’s Department to sign contract outside of the meeting. Commissioner Plaskett seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0. ROAD DEPARTMENT – Scooter Mentaberry, Supervisor

source_text: 1. Review, discuss and provide direction to the Comptroller related to proposed cost of living adjustments for Non-PERS and PERS employees, effective July 5, 2026. Note: Union contracts have not been approved for next year so COLA increase is unknown at this time. Elected Officials are limited to a 2% increase, County Commissioners are limited to a 3% increase. (For Possible Action) At the previous Commission meeting during the budget session the board chose to not approve a COLA increase for the County Commissioners, Comptroller Kim Todd informed the board that due to a new legislative bill they unfortunately can not approve some but not all. In order to follow new legislature the board either approves a COLA increase for all non-PERS and PERS employees, elected officials and County Commissioners or none at all. Commissioner Schoenwald motioned to approve a 2% COLA for elected officials, 3% for County Commissioners, 3% COLA for hourly employees and $0.25 increase for casual positions. Commissioner Plaskett seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0.

source_text: Process in lieu of Hiring Freeze Resolution. (For Possible Action) Director Lopez explained when it comes to revenue the County doesn’t need to put a hiring freeze in place, looking into the future they want to make sure that all positions are reviewed prior to approval or postings. Kim Todd commented on proposed changes to the draft Workforce Position Control and Vacancy Review Process in lieu of Hiring Freeze Resolution; adding if the position was budgeted for and what year, adding additional costs that a department head would not know about, get rid of the county manager authorization spot due to the county manager position being removed. Rewording that the Commissioners “shall” confirm funding with the Comptroller’s office, she also believes the board should always have the opportunity to authorize layoffs due to never knowing what kind of financial burden they may face. Vice Chair Plaskett commented the layoff section was meant to say that the resolution was not intended for layoffs. The board discussed proposed changes and re-wording of certain areas and bringing the resolution back onto a future agenda. No action was taken. TREASURER – Pernecia, Johnson, Treasurer

source_text: Impact Statement. (For Possible Action) The original record of decision was signed in 2012 and was appealed by an environmental group and a farming family in Diamond Valley; the 9th circuit vacated the case back to the BLM to address issues. The supplemental EIS process was issued a second record of decision in 2019 that was again appealed, the case went to the federal district court and eventually General Moly went bankrupt and a new company called New Molly LLC is continuing the case. The new Mount Hope Project Environmental Impact Statement discusses the amended plan of operation and redesigns facilities to avoid any use of occupancy of the withdrawn lands; however, the plan does not discuss how it will conform with the Greater Sage Grouse plans. The Board discussed reviewing the BLM state directors review of the record of decision and sending a letter to the company asking to reengage in conversations reminding them of their commitments to Eureka County. Vice Chair Plaskett motioned to approve reviewing the BLM state directors review of the record of decision and sending a formal letter to the company. Commissioner Schoenwald seconded the motion. source_snippet: (For Possible Action) The proposed changes to the Eureka County Personnel Policy: Leave Plans, 6.1 Holidays are: Employees participating in the 4x10 pilot program shall follow the existing Holiday Leave policy applicable to 10-hour workdays, except as modify below. For Offices required by Nevada law to remain operational, including elected official offices: If a federally recognized holiday falls on a Friday or Saturday, the elected official or department head may coordinate with employees to schedule an alternate day off. Any such holiday leave must be taken within the same work week in which the holiday occurs, ensuring that operational coverage is maintained. Commissioner Plaskett motioned to approve the changes to Eureka County Personnel Policy: Leave Plans, 6.1 Holidays. Commissioner Schoenwald seconded the motion. The motion carried 3- IT – Misty Rowley, CIO
source_text: (For Possible Action) The proposed changes to the Eureka County Personnel Policy: Leave Plans, 6.1 Holidays are: Employees participating in the 4x10 pilot program shall follow the existing Holiday Leave policy applicable to 10-hour workdays, except as modify below. For Offices required by Nevada law to remain operational, including elected official offices: If a federally recognized holiday falls on a Friday or Saturday, the elected official or department head may coordinate with employees to schedule an alternate day off. Any such holiday leave must be taken within the same work week in which the holiday occurs, ensuring that operational coverage is maintained. Commissioner Plaskett motioned to approve the changes to Eureka County Personnel Policy: Leave Plans, 6.1 Holidays. Commissioner Schoenwald seconded the motion. The motion carried 3- IT – Misty Rowley, CIO

source_text: 1. Report on current and emerging natural resource issues affecting Eureka County. (Discussion) Natural Resources Manager Jake Tibbitts reported the Rodent Board met and approved the borough builder rental agreement; members of the Rodent District can now come and rent the borough builder. The Rodent Board also approved a few cost share reimbursements. Manager Tibbitts attended the BLM Greater Sage Grouse Plan Implementation meeting with cooperating agencies; they are committed to developing a Memorandum of Understandings with the State and NDOW to clarify some of the grey areas moving forward. Manager Tibbitts gave a presentation to the Diamond Valley Groundwater Management Plan on the results of the Mining and Land Resource -- 12 of 299 -- Page 9 of 11- April 21, 2026 Institute meeting. Manager Tibbitts attended a meeting with ORLA Mining about the South Railroad project, they discussed the concerns Pine Valley residents had on the water issues, he believes they will be removing their protests on the water applications. Manager Tibbitts reminded the board Firewise days will be May 1st in Eureka and May 2nd in Crescent Valley.

source_snippet: 2. Pledge of Allegiance. The Board of Eureka County Commissioners met pursuant to law on May 5, 2026. Present were Chairman Rich McKay, Vice Chair Marty Plaskett, Commissioner Mike Schoenwald via Webex, District Attorney Ted Beutel and Deputy Clerk Recorder Katelyn Ziemann. The meeting was called to order at 9:30 a.m. The interactive video conferencing system was connected between Crescent Valley and Eureka for the entire meeting. Commissioner Plaskett motioned to approve the agenda with moving the Crescent Valley Town Board item up until after Public Comment. Commissioner Schoenwald seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0. The meeting began with the pledge of allegiance. PUBLIC COMMENT
source_text: 2. Pledge of Allegiance. The Board of Eureka County Commissioners met pursuant to law on May 5, 2026. The meeting was called to order at 9:30 a.m. The interactive video conferencing system was connected between Crescent Valley and Eureka for the entire meeting. Commissioner Plaskett motioned to approve the agenda with moving the Crescent Valley Town Board item up until after Public Comment. Commissioner Schoenwald seconded the motion. source_text: Commission Department (010-019-53010-000). (For Possible Action) -- 14 of 164 -- Page 12 of 13- May 19, 2026 The current Eureka County Master Plan has not been updated since 2010, Nevada’s Statute covers the requirement for a county to maintain a master plan that guides land use, growth management, infrastructure, economic development, natural resources, water resources and transportation. The Hazard Mitigation plan and other economic development planning is being updated, Director Rowley believes now would be a good time to include the Master Plan. Commissioner Plaskett motioned to approve a Contracted Services Agreement and Scope of Work between Eureka County and Nevada Strategies LLC for development of the Eureka County Master Plan and general planning advisory services for a term of twelve (12) months at $10,000.00 per month, for a total contract amount not to exceed $120,000.00, utilizing funds budgeted for contract services in the Public Works Department (010-042-53010-058) and services and supplies in the Planning Commission Department (010-019-53010-000). Commissioner Schoenwald seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0. CORRESPONDENCE

source_text: America 250 Project. (For Possible Action) The Charters of Freedom America 250 Project has donated to Eureka County fully engraved, stainless-steel replicas of the Declaration of Independence, US Constitution, Bill of Rights, and Civil Rights Amendments. The board along with Eureka citizens in the audience and members of the Eureka VFW discussed where the best location would be. The board chose the VFW Park for the location of the replicas; they discussed bringing the cost of the project to a later meeting but in the meantime direct NACO to work with Public Works Assistant Director Lester Porter for the delivery of the replicas. Commissioner Plaskett motioned to approve the VFW Park as the location for the replicas of the Declaration of Independence, US Constitution, Bill of Rights, and Civil Rights Amendments gifted to Eureka County by The Charters of Freedom America 250 Project, also to work further details with Eldon Allred with the VFW and Lester Porter. Commissioner Schoenwald seconded the motion. The motion carried 3-0.

source_text: For Possible Action: Approve the Lyon County Personnel Policy Manual with proposed revisions. Proposed revisions include: increase the period from 60 to 90 days as the time within which an employee must use compensatory time; change the definition for which employees are entitled to shift differential; increase vacation accrual from 40 hours to 80 hours for the first year; change various definitions; add a requirement that employees on administrative leave remain available for work; and other minor language clarifications, with all proposed revisions to be effective beginning July 1, 2026. (Human Resources Director, Ben Evans). Significant Changes: Increase compensatory time use time from 90 days to 120 calendar days. Defined only regular staff qualify for a shift differential. Increase vacation accrual from 40 hours to 80 hours during the first year of employment with the County. Defined requirements for personnel to qualify for personal day. Defined employees must exhaust all applicable paid time off before LWOP may be taken. Defined "regular commute distance" for mileage reimbursement purposes. source_text: 5.4.1 Lead Agency Coordination If a project advances beyond the concept planning phase, the lead agency for design and construction will typically be the County in which the project is located. The County would generally be responsible for project scoping, consultant procurement, local coordination, funding applications, design management, public outreach, permitting support, bidding, contract management, and construction administration. However, since these projects directly affect a Nevada State Route, NDOT coordination will be required. Depending on project location, funding source, ownership, maintenance responsibility, and anticipated impacts to state highway infrastructure, NDOT may serve as either a coordinating agency, review agency, funding partner, or lead agency. If NDOT cost-share participation is available, the County and NDOT should determine early in the implementation process which agency will lead project delivery.

source_text: 5.4.2 Federal-Aid Funding Considerations If Federal-aid Highway Program funds are used, the project must be developed in accordance with applicable federal requirements. In that case, NDOT would typically coordinate with FHWA to manage federal participation, ensure compliance with Federal-aid procedures, and administer required approvals. Federal requirements may include, but are not limited to, environmental documentation, right-of-way certification, utility coordination, disadvantaged business enterprise requirements, Buy America provisions, competitive procurement, construction contract administration, documentation, and reimbursement procedures. Early identification of the funding source is important because federal funding can affect project schedule, documentation requirements, procurement methods, and agency roles. Projects should not proceed into final design or construction advertisement until the applicable funding and compliance requirements are clearly established. -- 172 of 706 --

source_text: 7. NAC 477 – State Fire Marshall Under NAC 477.740, the Nevada State Fire Marshal Division is required to review fire-safety plans for certain building and construction projects to ensure compliance with the State’s adopted fire codes. This includes any building, construction project, or fire-protection system involving public occupancy in a county with a population under 100,000 when no interlocal agreement exists between the State Fire Marshal and the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ). Because Lyon County remains under 100,000 population, the regulation directly applies. If a project is submitted in an area outside the jurisdiction of a local fire-protection district, and the County does not have an interlocal agreement that delegates review authority, then the County must forward those plans to the State Fire Marshal for review and issuance of the required certificate of compliance. A structure cannot be occupied until the State Fire Marshal has issued this certificate. Furthermore, Lyon County’s adoption of the 2024 IFC and Northern Nevada Amendments to the IFC would align county code with the State Fire Marshall standards.

source_text: Based on the information available, the fiscal impact associated with Lyon County’s adoption of the 2024 International Fire Code (IFC) and the 2024 Northern Nevada Amendments to the IFC is generally expected to be minimal to none. Lyon County does not typically conduct plan reviews or inspections for fire code compliance, except in limited circumstances involving development located outside the jurisdictional boundaries of local fire protection districts. As a result, the adoption of the updated fire code provisions does not appear likely to create additional staffing requirements, operational burdens, or ongoing fiscal obligations for the County. The primary anticipated cost to the County is the acquisition of the updated IFC code books and related reference materials necessary to satisfy statutory requirements for public inspection. These expenses are limited in scope and appear to be one-time in nature. Planning and Coordination Throughout the ten-month engagement period, Lyon County Code Enforcement worked closely with the property owner and multiple partner agencies to develop a lawful, coordinated, and humane approach to restoring the property to a compliant condition. Coordination efforts addressed the following operational considerations: • Occupant notification procedures and legal compliance requirements • Safety planning and risk assessment • Human services resource outreach and engagement • Contractor selection and coordination • Debris removal logistics and environmental considerations • Law enforcement support and operational planning • Fire safety and environmental impact mitigation In early April 2026, the property owner finalized a contractual agreement with a local contractor to perform the cleanup and remediation of the site. source_snippet: For Possible Action: Approve the services of independent contractor Candice Landa, LCSW, in an amount not to exceed $84,500, to provide Behavioral Health Clinician services for the Lyon County Resilient Families (LCRF) program. Recommended revision Any onsite generation exceeding the lesser of:  10% of the data center’s maximum demand, or  emergency-only generation capacity,  should be deemed a principal power-generation use requiring a separate CUP. It is phased and cumulative. However, the draft permits review no more frequently than every five years. source_text: 19. Improve the decommissioning provisions The draft’s requirement for financial security equal to 150% of estimated decommissioning cost is commendably strong. It is phased and cumulative. However, the draft permits review no more frequently than every five years. That is too infrequent for rapidly changing equipment, battery disposal costs, inflation, and site conditions. Recommended changes  Review every two years.  Automatic annual inflation adjustment.  Independent estimate commissioned by the County.  No corporate guarantee as security.  Surety must be licensed and highly rated.  Letter of credit must be irrevocable and automatically renewable.  County may draw immediately upon abandonment, insolvency, nonrenewal, or failure to decommission.  Security must include demolition, hazardous materials, e-waste, soil and groundwater remediation, utility removal, roads, foundations, landscaping, and County administrative costs.  No two-year marketing extension unless the security remains fully funded.  Require partial decommissioning of abandoned phases even if other phases continue operating.  Require removal of underground foundations, conduits, tanks, and contaminate...

source_text: 22. Correct drafting inconsistencies The ordinance needs a careful legal and technical edit before introduction. Apparent issues include:  The title says data centers are being established as a “permitted use,” while the zoning table appears to use “C,” indicating conditional approval.  Definitions jump from number 16 to number 18.  The natural-gas accessory definition references “15.336.17.J.1.d,” although natural- gas facilities appear later under Section L.  Accessory BESS is initially defined as exclusively backup or emergency power and not grid-interconnected for sales, while later language allows “grid-stabilization,” load balancing, and peak reduction benefiting the broader grid.  The phrase “reasonably necessary” is undefined and grants excessive discretion.  Cooling towers are assigned setbacks even though water-consuming cooling towers are generally prohibited, creating ambiguity.  Numbering and lettering are inconsistent in several places.  The ordinance appears to allow the Director broad “alternative compliance” authority over screening without defined findings or public notice.  The parking standard of one space per 5,000 square feet may produce excessive...

source_text: 1. Setbacks A major concern I have with the ordinance is the proposed setbacks. The ordinance would allow data center buildings and emergency generators to be just 150 feet from homes. Substations could be 200 feet away, and battery energy storage systems and natural gas power facilities could be as close as 250 feet. How were these distances determined? The ordinance does not show that they are based on air pollution studies, health studies, noise studies, battery fire risks, emergency response times, or any other scientific evidence showing these distances are safe. A fence, wall, or landscaped buffer may hide the facility from view, but it does not stop air pollution, diesel exhaust, fine particulate matter (PM2.5), chemical releases, low-frequency noise, vibration, or contaminated smoke if there is a fire. Families should not have to live just a few hundred feet away from a massive industrial facility that operates 24 hours a day and stores large amounts of fuel, batteries, electrical equipment, and cooling chemicals.

source_text: The ordinance should also include stronger operating standards. The County should: Require pollution prevention before pollution control. The goal should not simply be to meet the minimum legal requirements. The goal should be to prevent unnecessary air pollution whenever possible. Prohibit diesel generators from being used for peak shaving, routine grid support, demand response, power sales, or reducing operating costs. Allow diesel generators only during a true power outage or limited maintenance and testing. Set enforceable limits on generator numbers, testing hours, operating hours, fuel use, and total emissions. Require testing to be staggered so multiple facilities are not operating generators at the same time. Require the cleanest available engines, pollution controls, and fuels. Simply labeling an engine "Tier 4" should not end the review. Require battery storage or other non-combustion backup systems whenever they can safely replace diesel generators. Diesel generators should be the last option, not the first.

The Lyon County Resilient Families (LCRF) Program performs evidence based assessments to determine need and level of care, targeted case management, prevention and early intervention, evidenced based parent education on substance use, and wrap around linkage to services for youth and families in Lyon County who are affected by Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) or at risk of OUD. Case Management and linkage to care is provided for members of families as well as treatment connection for individuals age 16 and over, with special consideration for transitional aged youth, and those involved or at risk for being involved with the criminal justice or juvenile justice system. The services of Candice Landa, LCSW will be up to 25 hours weekly to provide the Behavioral Health Clinician role for the LCRF program as covered in the State of Nevada, Health and Human Services, Directorâ€™s Office Fund for a Resilient Nevada grant award. The location of the Project along the alignment of the Corridors indicates that the County recognized this region as appropriate for new commercial/industrial development associated with additional electrical capacity. The following images depict an excerpt from the 2020 Master Plan and an image from the applicant (with staff modifications). The Corridors are 2/3 of a mile in width and are locations where Title 15 does not require a Conditional Use Permit for high voltage power lines. The intent of these corridors is to delineate areas that may connect to the NV Energy, State-wide, Greenlink project and the Walker River Substation expansion. The applicant will be pursing options with the NV Fish and Game Commission or with the project proponents of the Winston Solar PUD to the north of the Project area in order to attain easements for connection to the Walker River Substation complex. (Note that the dimensions for the Winston Solar project are not accurate in the second image: the solar array will extend closer to Hwy 95A than depicted.) source_text: V. Public Comment on the CCB Language Access Plan Chair Berry opened Item V for public comment. Amanda Connor spoke and stressed the importance of having a Language Access Plan given the difficulties her clients have experienced communicating with CCB agents on the prior matter. Chair Berry asked if staff had any comment to add. Julia Butler, Education Information Office and Language Access Liason for the CCB addressed the board and stated that pursuant to NRS 232.0081 the LAP is subject to public comment before being submitted. She addressed Amanda Connor and said that her clients are not responsible for providing translation services, the agency is. Ms. Butler said she is available to help facilitate those services. Ms. Butler said that updates to the document have not changed the process of assisting limited English proficiency individuals but modernizes current capabilities and goals. Chair Berry asked for any comments. Member Rath asked Ms. Butler how the CCB would address language needs that the CCB can’t internally support. Public Comment Steve Owens, of Oracle Corporation, said Oracle Corporation is now in the cannabis market and summarized they have a regulatory ecosystem which includes automated licensing, embedded compliance and enforcement, case management and embedded AI. He expressed interest in discussing seed-to-sale, track-and-trace and future possibilities of the CCB and Oracle’s regulatory, integrated platform. He noted there are medical benefits to using cannabis, but the package label should include warnings that these solvents can cause serious side effects to the user. Additionally, Mr. Elgus stated his belief that if a complaint is filed, the complainant should receive a summary of the outcome of the complaint and investigation. There were no additional public comments. Chair Berry noted a written public comment was received via email from Dan and that it will be introduced into public comment.

source_text: For Possible Action: To approve an agreement with Sierra Controls, in an amount not to exceed $160,216.25, to migrate the Silver Springs Wastewater Treatment Plant's existing SCADA system to a new SCADA platform. (Utilities Director, Sean Sinclair) The utility-wide SCADA system has experienced ongoing reliability issues, and the FY27 budget includes funding for a SCADA Improvement Project. Before the project could begin, an electrical storm caused a complete failure of the SCADA computer at the Silver Springs Plant, significantly impacting plant operations. To restore reliable operational control, staff and the Consultant recommend beginning the SCADA improvement work at Silver Springs immediately. The work will include replacing the failed computers and migrating the existing system to the recommended Ignition SCADA platform. The upgraded system can later be integrated into the utility-wide SCADA network as improvements are completed at other facilities. Sierra Controls, the utilityâ€™s SCADA consultant, will provide the hardware and software, perform the migration, and train utility staff. source_text: For Possible Action: To approve an agreement with Sierra Controls, in an amount not to exceed $160,216.25, to migrate the Silver Springs Wastewater Treatment Plant's existing SCADA system to a new SCADA platform. (Utilities Director, Sean Sinclair) The utility-wide SCADA system has experienced ongoing reliability issues, and the FY27 budget includes funding for a SCADA Improvement Project. Before the project could begin, an electrical storm caused a complete failure of the SCADA computer at the Silver Springs Plant, significantly impacting plant operations. To restore reliable operational control, staff and the Consultant recommend beginning the SCADA improvement work at Silver Springs immediately. The work will include replacing the failed computers and migrating the existing system to the recommended Ignition SCADA platform. The upgraded system can later be integrated into the utility-wide SCADA network as improvements are completed at other facilities. Sierra Controls, the utilityâ€™s SCADA consultant, will provide the hardware and software, perform the migration, and train utility staff. plain_english_explanation: 2. PUBLIC COMMENT Ms. Ferris entertained public comments. Carre Mofhitz-Paugh introduced herself as a Carson City resident residing at 528 Ruby Lane in Carson City located directly in front of the Applicant’s property. Ms. Mofhitz-Paugh shared concerns regarding ongoing flooding issues affecting her home. She explained that approximately six years ago, stormwater began flooding her backyard and house following excavation work by a neighbor and the City. She added that despite mitigation efforts, the flooding issue remained after two years. Ms. Mofhitz-Paugh noted that she had video documentation of the flooding, specifically from a hail storm in June 2023. She requested that a drainage study be conducted before new construction takes place.

one_sentence_summary: 5. PUBLIC COMMENT
plain_english_explanation: 5. PUBLIC COMMENT (8:33:51) – Mayor Bagwell entertained public comments. Mark Costa commented on the tentative budget, which the Board would approve at its next Special Meeting on May 27, 2025. He pointed out areas of concern, such as the Workers’ Compensation Fund, the Insurance Fund, the Regional Transportation Fund, and the Street Maintenance Fund, which he believed showed deficits. He also requested that the Board review the General Fund and take corrective action. Deni French noted that he was “anxious about our bug population” and wished to see oases in the City to preserve the bug population. He also suggested checking out all the tied-down trees to ensure they have “room to budge” and to pull them out if they have been unable to stand on their own for two years or more. Mr. French suggested pulling item 11.e from the Consent Agenda.

source_text: 5. PUBLIC COMMENT (8:31:58) – Mayor Bagwell entertained public comments. Deni French noted that he had attended several City Commission/Committee meetings and had “come to the conclusion that it’s very complicated for me.” He noted that he had planned to connect with Parks, Recreation, and Open Space staff to ensure he was prepared prior to getting to a meeting. Mr. French also suggested combining the Open Space Advisory Committee (OSAC) and the Parks and Recreation Commission (PRC). He also referenced an article in the Nevada Appeal regarding creating protection and migration paths for the Monarch Butterfly. Battle Born Tree Service Owner Michael Orlick expressed concern regarding companies that have been providing tree services that “are not legitimate.” He recommended requiring a contractor’s license which is not required in Nevada at this time. Mr. Orlick noted that they have invested in equipment and are being underbid by “people doing business illegally,” adding that he was required to have a contractor’s license in California but not in Nevada. Mayor Bagwell stated that Staff would be in touch with him regarding the concern.

source_text: 5. PUBLIC COMMENT (8:34:11) – Mayor Bagwell entertained public comments. Carson City Parks, Recreation, and Open Space Senior Natural Resource Specialist Marenna Lovejoy announced several volunteer programs such as Move with the Mayor on September 28, 2024, at Lone Mountain Cemetery for “cleanup work” and the volunteer appreciation event at Silver Saddle Ranch on October 12, 2024. Ms. Lovejoy also suggested taking the Carson River User Experience and the Centennial Park Master Plan surveys. Mayor Bagwell encouraged volunteer groups to help maintain sections of the Lone Mountain Cemetery all year round. Paula Peters spoke against Carson City selling water rights. She also objected to using artificial turf at Centennial Park due to its toxicity and likelihood of causing injuries. Deni French also objected to agenda items 14.a and 15.a and offered to provide research proving the hazards of artificial turf. He believed that the additional heat caused by artificial turf was damaging to children’s health and stated that he would begin researching the hazards of microplastics.

source_text: 5. PUBLIC COMMENT (8:35:57) – Mayor Bagwell entertained public comments. Deni French expressed concern that during last Sunday’s Red Flag Warning, no signage was placed by the Open Space Division at the Prison Hill OHV area and near Golden Eagle Lane. He thanked Supervisor Schuette for bringing his concerns to the Open Space team and the Fire Chief. Dani Mulevicz introduced herself as the President of the Kings Canyon Meadows Homeowners’ Association (HOA) and expressed her support for any financial resources given to the wildlands fire crews. She also thanked the Carson City Fire Department (CCFD) for partnering with the Kings Canyon Meadows HOA to assist in their defensible space projects. Deborah Case introduced herself as the coordinator of the Firewise Program for Kings Canyon Meadows HOA and concurred with Ms. Mulevicz’s comments. She thanked the CCFD for helping them become a Fire Adaptive community and for helping them with dumpsters during brush clearing times and wished to support all the funding the CCFD wished to request.

Ryan Russell also recommended Ms. Bruketta to be appointed as Justice of the Peace. Sena Loyd advocated for the appointment of Melanie Bruketta as well. source_text: 7. PUBLIC COMMENT (5:34:37) – Chairperson Novak entertained final public comments. Mark Costa addressed item 5.A, and suggested that the survey questions could be used for public outreach and to receive public input on prioritization. He was also pleased to see that the PCI Report had been completed, as it impacted the Transportation Plan. He wished to see the reversal of the deterioration that had been going on for the past 10 years. Director of The Rural Center for Independent Living Dee Dee Foremaster suggested “tapping into the medical transportation money” in Medicaid to be used to transport Lyon County residents. She also wished to see the new bus stops become more accessible for the visually impaired and for those who need benches to sit on. Ms. Foremaster offered to have the surveys filled out by the community she serves. Ms. Walt read a written statement regarding the Nevada Rural RSVP Program’s lead in establishing a collaboration group with stakeholders to address key transportation issues in the Quad-County region. She invited key stakeholders and participants to get in touch with her by emailing to mwalt@nvrsp.org.

source_text: 3. PUBLIC COMMENT (4:32:43) – Chairperson Bagwell entertained public comments. Deni French wished to have this Board consider his concerns regarding “curb, sidewalks, bus stops, and steep driveways…without messing with the ADA compliance deals.” He also objected to the asphalting of the old V&T rail tracks. Executive Director of the Rural Center for Independent Living Dee Dee Foremaster expressed “grave concerns” -- 1 of 5 -- CARSON AREA METROPOLITAN PLANNING ORGANIZATION Minutes of the July 10, 2024 Meeting Page 2 about the sidewalks. Ms. Foremaster cited the example of a construction project on King Street where both sides of the sidewalk were being worked on and her husband had gone on the unblocked sidewalk and was barely missed by construction equipment. She recommended working on one side of the sidewalk and not on both sides. Melinda Cash introduced herself as the Chair of the Mound House Advisory Board and updated the Board on the meetings that had been conducted regarding safety. She recommended a reduction in the speed limit [on US Highway 50] to 35 miles per hour in Mound House.

source_text: I. Public Comment Will Adler thanked the CCB for the meeting and stated he submitted written comments for consideration. Glenn Miller asked for clarification on how to speak on issues during public comment during this meeting. Deputy Director Miles responded that the public is permitted to comment on the regulations as each agenda item as discussed. Deputy Director Miles introduced Director James Humm. Director Humm thanked everyone in attendance for their time and participation during these meetings. Director Humm provided an overview of the comprehensive study and emerging sector analysis survey which is underway, and encouraged consumer and industry participation to aid in understanding how the industry can be improved. Director Humm affirmed that information collected will remain confidential and individual responses will not be shared publicly or privately with the State of Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board or anyone other than the independent research team. Director Humm stated that survey findings will be included in a publicly available report when it is complete.

During public comment, Mac Rossi shared concerns regarding restroom availability at Paradise Park and suggested that portable restrooms be funded year-round rather than continuing repairs to existing facilities. He also suggested considering a funding mechanism tied to new housing development to support park improvements in areas experiencing growth. Mr. Rossi thanked staff for upcoming youth fishing activities at the park, described community gardening and Arbor Day projects being organized with a nearby school, and expressed appreciation for recent traffic and safety improvements along Carville Avenue.

Note: The proposed allocation of the tax rate must be submitted to the Department of Taxation. (For Possible Action) owners would only go up 3% regardless of how much an increase is made to the tax rate. Comptroller Todd noted the rules and guidelines set by the State of Nevada for a rate increase adding that the State needs to know by February 21 st and that the Board needs to act today so that all deadlines can be met in a timely manner. Crescent Valley audience member Jeremy Rice added that it is important that the Board get the details and information for a rate increase out to the public. source_text: III. Public Comment. Deputy Director Miles opened Agenda Item III and asked for public comment in Las Vegas. Will Adler stated his appreciation for the discussion of lot size at the start of the meeting and said he has discussed the issue with cultivators, all who expressed a desire for increased lot size. He said he agrees that labs should be protected but said that there is more than one business model for a cultivator, not just those who are big, or vertically integrated. Mr. Adler said continued conversation will benefit the industry. Tina Schellinger said she appreciates and recognizes the lowering of agent card costs for renewal or replacement and would like to see the system streamlined for recordkeeping purposes. Ms. Schellinger said it is positive to eliminate excessive testing for products that are going in production and will get blasted because it is redundant. There were no additional public comments in Las Vegas or online.

source_text: 7. PUBLIC COMMENT (5:07:47) – Chairperson Bagwell entertained final public comments. Mr. French expressed concerns regarding the Carson Wandering Skipper, stating that their habitat was diminishing. He emphasized that the City has a responsibility to protect the insect since it was endangered. Mr. French added that the City should protect species that are close to endangerment. He inquired about new bus stop designs for safety and sheltering purposes. Mr. French noted that he hoped the federal funds could be used for street ramps. (5:11:04) – Dee Dee Foremaster of the Rural Center for Independent Living said that the Highway 50 area near Classy Seconds was in desperate need of a bus stop. Ms. Foremaster said there were several community organizations in the area and the closest bus stop was half a mile away, so individuals had to walk up U.S. Highway 50 with walkers and wheelchairs to access the bus services. (4:01:36) – Eric Brooks, Arts & Culture Program Manager for Visit Carson City, informed the Commission that Visit Carson City was awarded an $18,000 grant through the America 250 grant cycle. He explained that the funds will support a project called “Points of Unity,” which is part of a larger initiative known as the “Dust & Wonder Trail.” This program aims to unite Carson Valley, Virginia City, and Carson City as a single destination for visitors. Mr. Brooks outlined plans to install nine 53-inch railroad spikes at key locations, including Brewery Arts Center, Page 1 Minutes Carson City Historic Resources Commission January 7, 2026 Stewart Indian School, Wungnema House, V&T Railroad Depot, Dat-So-La-Lee House, Carson River Park, Carson Hot Springs, McFadden Plaza, and the Historic Nevada State Prison. Each spike will feature an interactive QR code that, when scanned, displays a map of the entire region. He noted that installations are anticipated in May of 2026, with completion by June 30, 2026, and emphasized that the V&T Railroad serves as a vital connector for the three regions.

source_text: 15. Public Comment** Jay Giovacchini announced that CERT is trying to prep and ready as many volunteers as possible for a potential emergency shelter set up. A meeting and training session will take place in January 2026. Red Cross procedures and policies were reviewed and walked through the shelter trailers. If there is interest in learning about shelter trailers, information is available. The idea behind it, is if a shelter needs to be set up and can be expensive, and Red Cross is needed from the beginning, the expense does not come back onto Carson City. Bakkedahl states that a next meeting scheduled will be set up during a weekday so all departments can join. Parks and Rec need to be present because they are the key holders. Acting Fire Chief, Kevin Nyberg states that Carson City emails and website will change from “carson.org” to “carsoncity.com” in the new year. Steve Funk states that the community and the public need to be made aware when contacting the city.

He also mentioned a book called Burnt and that he had a season with the Department of Forestry, and people would possibly find interest in this program. Firefighter’s suits and uniforms have a great jump right now in technology and it would be great to review them.

Robyn Orloff introduced herself as a Carson City resident and shared a recent cycling experience along the Odyssey Trail, Desert Peach Trail, and Riverview Trail and expressed appreciation for Open Space’s efforts on the trails. Ms. Orloff supported the idea of Members participating in events and visiting Open Space areas to better understand the public’s perspective. She requested annual reviews of sensitive resources including “the waterfall, double waterfall crawler route, off-the-trailer crawler route, and lower headlight open area,” noting that these areas weren’t included in Bureau of Land Management’s report. Ms. Orloff highlighted the need for closer monitoring of ephemeral streams and sensitive hydrological and vegetation resources. She added that she witnessed destruction of intact resources during events and shared the documentation with Open Space but had not received a response. Ms. Orloff emphasized the importance of accountability to address impacts from events. She encouraged the Committee to include public perspectives and site visits in annual evaluations. one_sentence_summary: 9. PUBLIC COMMENT
plain_english_explanation: 9. PUBLIC COMMENT (8:46:51) – Chairperson McDermott entertained public comments. Denny French expressed disappointment that the report did not address the need to replace approximately 200 trees and the estimated cost. He stated that some of the tree stress resulted from neglect, including lack of water, pruning, and timely observation, and that earlier involvement of an arborist may have changed outcomes. He requested clarification regarding responsibility for tree maintenance and stated he does not support funding new tree plantings until an arborist is hired and responsibilities are defined. He also reiterated concern about the condition of the cemetery and asked that it receive attention. Mr. French stated he was dissatisfied with some of the responses, and lack thereof, he has received regarding these issues.

STAFF REPORTS (NON-ACTION ITEMS) - DIRECTOR'S REPORT TO THE COMMISSION (6:19:21) – Ms. Sullivan requested feedback from the Commission on public feedback. - FUTURE AGENDA ITEMS (6:19:52) – Ms. Sullivan noted that the next meeting’s agenda would include Special Use Permits for a guest building and to modify a wireless tower, a request for a variance, and the rezoning of the Northgate building. - COMMISSIONER REPORTS/COMMENTS (6:20:28) – Commissioner Borders believed it was “totally unacceptable to have somebody from the Building Department come up and tell me they’re too busy to get their building permit renewed and to Page 6 Minutes Carson City Planning Commission January 31, 2024 waste our time going through a permit again because they were quote too busy to make sure that it happened,” calling it disrespectful. Chair Preston was surprised to see that the trailer was placed at a City site before it was approved. Vice Chair Loyd wished to see some of the Master Plan public meetings take place at night. Chair Preston believed Saturday meetings could be more effective.

one_sentence_summary: 6. Consideration of Subcommittee Name Revision to Reflect Codified Statutory Reference (Information, Discussion, and for Possible Action)
plain_english_explanation: 6. Consideration of Subcommittee Name Revision to Reflect Codified Statutory Reference (Information, Discussion, and for Possible Action) Chair Braxton introduced the idea of updating the subcommittee’s name to reflect the codified statute now guiding its work, rather than referencing the original Assembly Bill (AB 469). Deputy Superintendent Ford recommended shortening the name to simply reflect "NRS 388G" instead of listing the full statute range, as the provisions may be amended in the future. After brief discussion, the members agreed to rename the subcommittee the NRS 388G Subcommittee to align with current statutory language and to clarify its purpose. Motion to change the name of the AB 469 Subcommittee to the NRS 388G Subcommittee. Motion by Chair Braxton, seconded by Member Hudson. Motion passed unanimously.

Category-specific percentages included: Medicaid at 13.1%, SNAP at 26.0%, TANF at 0.1%, Homeless at 1.0%, Foster at 0.22%, and Migrant at 0.0%. Order to Show Cause for Strive Wellness of Nevada, LLC (C206, P131) (TOI #24001) (for possible action) David Staley stated item A is in order to show cause why the Board should not deny a TOI application for Strive Wellness of Nevada. On July 25, 2023, the Board approved a stipulated settlement agreement which required 2 of the 3 owners of Strive, Lawrence Lemons and Donald Burton to submit a TOI and sell their ownership interest within 6 months. On January 17, 2024, Lemons submitted a TOI application 24001, requesting approval to sell strives nonoperational cultivation and production licenses to Item 9 Labs Corp., however, TOI number 24001 was incomplete as filed because it did not include required signatures from Burton and Sarah Gullickson, 2 of the 3 Strive owners. one_sentence_summary: III. Public Comment
plain_english_explanation: III. Public Comment Washoe County Assessor Chris Sarman made public comment expressing concerns regarding State Board Case no. 25-152 (Empire Southwest). The State Board decided at the September 2025 meeting that leased assets labeled as CAT equipment were exempt despite evidence showing that some of the equipment was generating rental income. Assessor Sarman cited NRS 361.159 and stated that if exempt property was leased and or used for profit that a taxable interest existed. He asked that the State Board members strongly consider the new advisory opinion which not only affected the Washoe County Assessor’s office but the Elko and Humboldt County Assessor’s offices as well. Chief Deputy Roberts-Larson read the rules for hearings and administered the oath to those testifying.
